lessons.title: Key Takeaways and Where to Go Next

children.text: Five chapters, four case studies, and one recurring pattern: a strategy that looks profitable on paper and a real market that charges for every assumption a backtest quietly gets wrong. Before moving into the capstone, this lesson pulls the course's arc, formulas, and throughline into one place.
The Arc of This Course, in One Table

body.caption: Five chapters, five questions, five results

cells: Why does a backtest's return differ from what you actually earn?
A 22.4% backtest returned 4.1% live; transaction costs, spread, and market impact accounted for 37.2%, 22.4%, and 40.4% of the gap
What exactly does the government, the exchange, and the broker charge?
Six charges, priced and coded; a Bank Nifty scalp lost 91.3% of gross profit to explicit costs alone
What does the market itself charge, beyond published rates?
Spread and the square-root impact law, plus a momentum-specific drift cost that was the largest single component in its case study
How does trading frequency change everything above?
Cost drag = turnover x round-trip cost; a higher gross CAGR strategy lost to a lower one once turnover was accounted for
How do I build (and check) a backtest I can trust?
A four-category checklist; methodology bugs alone inflated one backtest's CAGR by over 6 points

cards.definition: Cost Drag (% per year) = Turnover Ratio x Round-Trip Cost (%). The annual erosion a strategy's turnover applies to its gross return, from Chapter 4.
T = 250 / H. Annual turnover ratio equals roughly 250 (NSE trading days per year) divided by average holding period in trading days, from Chapter 4.
Break-Even Gross CAGR = Turnover Ratio x Round-Trip Cost (%), the same figure as cost drag, read as a minimum threshold a strategy must clear, ideally with a 2x to 3x safety margin, from Chapter 4.
I = k x sigma x sqrt(Q / ADV). Market impact scales with the square root of participation rate (order value over average daily traded value), not linearly with order size, from Chapter 3.

children.text: Underneath five chapters of formulas and case studies, three habits do almost all of the work. First, never trust a cost function until it reproduces a number you already worked out by hand, the discipline used from Chapter 2 onward. Second, treat turnover as the master variable, since it multiplies every other cost this course has priced, explicit and implicit alike, at once. Third, separate cost problems from methodology problems, a perfect cost model bolted onto a look-ahead-biased gross return is still a broken backtest, as Chapter 5 showed directly.

body.text: None of this requires exotic tools. Every calculation in this course was ordinary arithmetic and a handful of Python functions, applied consistently and checked against known numbers. The edge this course builds is discipline, not complexity.

children.text: Where to Go Next: The Capstone

Chapter 6 closes the course by moving from backtest to reality: why live trading still costs more than even a fully realistic backtest predicts, a single audit framework that ties every tool from this course together into one repeatable process, how cost and slippage questions actually show up in quant and prop trading interviews, and a final, comprehensive case study that runs a strategy through the complete framework end to end.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A strategy has a turnover ratio of 8.0x and a round-trip cost of 0.25%. Using the formulas from this course, what is its break-even gross CAGR?
body.explanation: Break-Even Gross CAGR = Turnover Ratio x Round-Trip Cost = 8.0 x 0.25% = 2.00%. This strategy needs at least a 2.00% gross CAGR just to avoid losing money to costs, and following Chapter 4, ideally 4.00% to 6.00% (a 2x to 3x margin) before being considered live-ready.

body.text: A backtest is not a prediction, it is a claim, and every chapter in this course has been about the discipline of checking that claim before trusting it with real capital: price the costs precisely, model the slippage honestly, respect what turnover does to both, and make sure the methodology generating the gross return was sound in the first place.

points: This course built four independent disciplines: explicit costs (Chapter 2), slippage and market impact (Chapter 3), turnover and break-even analysis (Chapter 4), and backtest methodology integrity (Chapter 5), each shown capable of independently invalidating a backtest.
The core formulas, Cost Drag = Turnover x Round-Trip Cost, T = 250/H, and the square-root market impact law, apply across every strategy type and every chapter's case studies.
The habit that mattered more than any single formula was validating every model against a number already worked out by hand, and never trusting a cost estimate that skipped that step.
Chapter 6 closes the course with the paper-to-live transition, a unified audit framework, how these questions surface in quant and prop trading interviews, and one final end-to-end case study.
